body.x: Every Shia family knows the scene: the search has been going on for months, the introductions have not worked out, and someone — a mother, usually, at the end of a long evening — says, let us at least make dua properly. She is right, and the tradition she reaches for is rich and specific. Shia Islam has beloved verses and supplications for exactly this need, a defined place for istikhara, and a clear teaching about how dua works alongside effort. This guide gathers the ones that are well known and reliably sourced, and says honestly what each is for.
The verse almost every family recites: Quran 25:74

The most loved marriage dua in the Quran is the prayer of the servants of the Merciful in Surah al-Furqan: "Rabbana hablana min azwajina wa dhurriyyatina qurrata a'yunin waj'alna lil-muttaqina imama" — "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us a leader for the righteous" (25:74). Notice what it asks for. Not simply a spouse, but qurrat al-'ayn — coolness of the eyes, the deep settled joy a righteous partner and children bring. Parents recite it for their children, and those searching recite it for themselves; it is short enough to say after every prayer, and many families make it the fixed dua of the whole search.
Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us a leader for the righteous. — Quran 25:74
Two more Quranic prayers that belong in this search

When Musa (as), alone and without means in Madyan, had helped two women at a well and then sat in the shade, he prayed: "Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir" — "My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me" (28:24). The story continues with an invitation into a household and, in time, marriage. Scholars and families alike have loved this dua for the unmarried ever since, because it does not bargain or specify — it admits need and leaves the form of the good to Allah. It suits the searcher who is tired of writing lists of conditions.

And there is the prayer of Zakariya (as), who asked despite age and circumstance: "Rabbi la tadharni fardan wa anta khayrul-warithin" — "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors" (21:89). For the person who fears the search has simply gone on too long — the older searcher, the divorced or widowed, the one watching siblings marry one by one — this verse gives the fear a voice inside the prayer itself, which is often the most honest place to put it.

Mafatih al-Jinan, the collection of supplications compiled by Shaykh Abbas Qummi and found in nearly every Shia home, is less a book of single-purpose duas than a rhythm of prayer across days, nights and months — and the tradition's advice for someone seeking a spouse is largely to step into that rhythm with the intention carried inside it. Families commonly keep up the well-known supplications of the week, the dua for Friday, and the whispered prayers of the Imams, asking Allah for a righteous marriage within them rather than hunting for a formula. Dua al-Tawassul, the much-loved supplication seeking intercession through the Prophet and the Ahl al-Bayt (as), is recited in many homes on Tuesday nights, and a personal need — including marriage — is exactly the kind of haja it is customary to hold in mind and name at its close.
Parents' duas, and the times doors open widest

In Shia teaching a parent's prayer for a child carries a particular weight, and in practice it is often a mother's and father's duas — made quietly, over years, at times their child never sees — that families credit when a good match finally arrives. If you are a parent, the search is partly yours: your dua after obligatory prayers, in the last part of the night, and on the nights of Laylatul Qadr in Ramadan is not a small contribution but, many would say, the largest one available to you.

Certain times are loved for all duas and are natural anchors for this one: after each wajib prayer, when the heart is already turned; on Friday, which holds an hour in which supplication is answered; during the nights of Qadr, when families stay up in prayer anyway; on the night of the 15th of Sha'ban; and in the pause before breaking a fast, when the fasting person's dua is famously not turned away. Anchoring the marriage dua to these moments stops it depending on mood — it becomes part of the week's structure for as long as the search lasts.
Istikhara: its proper place, and its limits

Istikhara belongs in this picture, but in its proper place — which is later than many people put it. The istikhara of the Shia tradition is a prayer for guidance made after a real option exists and has been properly considered: a specific proposal, investigated, discussed with family, weighed by reason and counsel, where the heart still hesitates between two permissible paths. It is not a device for deciding whether to search, nor a substitute for checking a prospective spouse's character and references, nor something to repeat until it returns the answer already wanted. Families who use it well do the human work first — enquiry, meetings, honest questions — and then, at the genuine fork, ask Allah to incline the heart and open the way, accepting the outcome with a settled mind.
The etiquette: dua is paired with effort

The tradition is unambiguous that supplication and striving travel together. A dua for a spouse made while refusing every introduction, hiding from the community matchmaker, or never telling anyone that one is searching is only half a prayer. The etiquette, as families have practised it for generations, looks like this: pray the verses above with presence, not as a transaction; keep the search active and honest alongside them; give a little sadaqah with the intention of the need; accept introductions graciously even when unsure, because the answer to a dua rarely announces itself as one; and when a door closes, treat the closure as part of the answer rather than a failure of the prayer. The one making dua is asking for a righteous spouse, not a specified person on a specified date — and families who hold it that way find the waiting itself becomes bearable, and sometimes even fruitful.

excerpt: The actual duas Shia Muslims recite when seeking a spouse — Quran 25:74, the prayers of Musa and Zakariya, the Mafatih tradition, istikhara's proper place, and why dua is always paired with effort.
